title: If only — conditions, regrets and how sure you are
goal: Make plans with conditions (*kalau, jika*), talk about things that did not happen (*seandainya, coba kalau*), and say how sure you are (*pasti, mungkin, barangkali*). Indonesian does all of it without changing the verb — the little words carry the whole load.
bekal: plan with conditions: *Kalau hujan deras, kita tunggu di homestay*
regret what did not happen: *Coba kalau aku bawa jaket!*, *Seandainya aku tahu…*
grade your certainty from *pasti* through *mungkin* to *belum tentu*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Rencana ke Dieng
dialogs.intro: Early February, lunch break at the office. Mas Bayu has been talking for weeks about taking Sarah to the Dieng Plateau, two thousand metres up in the mountains of Central Java, to see the sunrise from Bukit Sikunir.

lines.text: Coba kalau Rina di Jogja, dia pasti ikut. Dia suka banget naik gunung.

lines.text: Ajak saja lain kali, Mbak. Dieng nggak akan ke mana-mana.

notes: **Kalau — the everyday "if".** Indonesian conditionals keep the verb exactly as it is: *Kalau hujan, kita tunggu* covers "if it rains, we'll wait" and "if it rained, we'd wait" alike. Time words and *pasti, mungkin, nanti* do the work that English does with *will, would, had*.

**Jika** in Bayu's quotation is the written "if", the one you find in terms and conditions, regulations and exam instructions. Nobody chatting about a weekend says *jika*, which is why Sarah laughs *Formal banget*. The whole sentence is a small lesson in notice language: *tamu, membatalkan, pesanan, tidak dapat dikembalikan*.

**Pasti and barangkali** sit at two ends of the certainty scale. *Pasti* is "definitely, surely" — and Indonesians use it freely, sometimes about things that are merely likely. *Barangkali* is "perhaps, probably", a touch softer and more old-fashioned than *mungkin*.

**Hangus — "burnt".** A forfeited deposit, an expired ticket or unused phone credit is *hangus*: gone, like toast. *Tiketnya hangus kalau tidak dipakai.* It is a word you will meet in the small print of every airline and phone plan.

**Seandainya and coba kalau** talk about things that are not real. *Seandainya Mbak Nur ikut* — supposing she came (she isn't coming). *Coba kalau Rina di Jogja* — if only she were here (she isn't). Neither needs a special verb form; the context makes it hypothetical.

**Nggak akan ke mana-mana — "won't go anywhere".** *Ke mana-mana* is "everywhere" (*Dia pergi ke mana-mana*), and with a negative it means "anywhere". 💬 *Subuh* is the dawn prayer time, and in everyday talk it simply means "at the crack of dawn", around half past four in Java.

grammars.title: If: kalau, jika, apabila, asal
body: All of these introduce a condition. The difference is register: *kalau* for talking, *jika* and *apabila* for writing, *asal* when the condition is the minimum you need.

head: Word
Register
Example
English
rows: In the event of fire, use the emergency stairs.
You can come, as long as you get up early.
In that case, I'll book now.

after: Order is free: the *kalau* clause can come first (with a comma) or second (usually without): *Kita tunggu di homestay kalau hujan.*
*Kalau* also means "when" for future events you expect: *Kalau sudah sampai, kabari aku, ya* (let me know when you've arrived). Nobody doubts you will arrive.

grammars.title: How sure are you?
body: Put these words before the verb or adjective, or at the start of the sentence. They are the Indonesian substitute for "will definitely", "might" and "probably won't".

head: Word
How sure
Example
English
rows: I'm afraid the road may be closed.

after: *Belum tentu* — "not yet certain" — is the polite way to disagree with someone's *pasti*: *Mahal pasti bagus?* — *Belum tentu.* (Expensive means good? — Not necessarily.)

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Coba kalau bawa jaket
dialogs.intro: Saturday, 4.15 in the morning, at the foot of Bukit Sikunir. Sarah's ten-degrees-is-nothing confidence has not survived the wind. A woman is selling knitted hats and gloves from a basket by the path.

lines.text: Iya, iya! Mudah-mudahan nggak berkabut, supaya kita bisa lihat Sindoro.

notes: **Coba kalau — "if only".** Literally "try if": try imagining the world in which I'd brought my jacket. It expresses regret about the past or a wish about the present, and it is the most natural way to say "if only" in conversation. *Coba kalau aku tahu dari dulu!* (If only I'd known sooner!)

**No past-tense trick needed.** *Coba kalau tadi aku bawa* — the verb *bawa* is the same one you would use for "I bring". *Tadi* (earlier) puts it in the past, *pasti* supplies the "would", and *nggak menggigil begini* makes clear it didn't happen.

**Sedingin ini — "this cold".** *Se-* + adjective + *ini/itu* means "as … as this/that": *semahal itu* (that expensive), *sebesar ini* (this big). You met *seramai* ("as busy as") in Unit 12, and Unit 16 is full of *se-* words.

**Kan kemarin sudah kuingatkan.** *Kan* here means "as you know, as I told you" — a gentle reproach. *Kuingatkan* is *aku* + *ingatkan* written as one word, a written and slightly literary habit (*kubaca, kukirim*); in speech most people would say *aku ingetin*.

**Anget and kupluk.** 💬 *Anget* is the spoken form of *hangat* (warm). *Kupluk* is a knitted beanie, the unofficial uniform of Dieng, where they are sold on every corner and worn even by the stall-holders' dogs.

**Keburu and mudah-mudahan.** *Keburu* 💬 means that something will happen before you manage to stop it: *keburu terbit* (it'll have risen before we get there), *keburu habis* (it'll be sold out). *Mudah-mudahan* is "hopefully", a softer, homelier twin of *semoga*.

grammars.title: Things that did not happen
body: Indonesian marks the unreal with a word at the front, not with the verb. Choose by feeling: wistful, hypothetical or plain regret.

head: Pattern
Example
English
rows: If only I'd brought a jacket.
If I'd known, I'd have brought it.
If only I had a car…
Had I known it'd be like this, I wouldn't have come.
Luckily I did bring an umbrella.

after: *Seandainya* is also for pure imagination about the future: *Seandainya aku menang lotre, aku beli rumah di Dieng.* Whether it means "if I won" or "if I had won" is left to context — and Indonesians find that perfectly clear.

blocks.text: *Kalau* is one of the hardest-working words in spoken Indonesian. Besides "if" and "when", it introduces a topic, sets up a comparison and softens a statement.

head: Use
Example
English
rows: Let me know when you get there.
As for me, I prefer coffee.
I like it spicy, whereas she doesn't.
If I remember rightly, he lives in Kotagede.
If you can, come before eight.

blocks.text: *Kalau nggak salah* and *kalau bisa* are politeness tools: the first makes a fact sound modest, the second turns an order into a wish. Mbak Nur uses *kalau bisa* the way a sergeant uses "now".
Plans in Java between November and March are made around the rain, so these words turn up in every trip conversation. Note *hujan* combining with other words, and the *ber-* adjectives for weather.

blocks.title: Useful at a homestay
items: *Ada air panas?* — Is there hot water? (In Dieng, ask before you book.)
*Sarapannya jam berapa?* — What time is breakfast?
*Boleh titip tas di sini?* — Can I leave my bag here?
*Kalau mau ke Sikunir, sebaiknya berangkat jam berapa?* — If we want to go to Sikunir, what time should we leave?

That's right. Has the meeting finished?
